lessonTitle: The Real Brayton Cycle: Efficiencies and Optimum Pressure Ratio

blocks.text: A jet engine for a small business aircraft must be both light and fuel-efficient. Its designer picks a compressor pressure ratio around 25, yet a ground-power gas turbine of the same turbine-entry temperature may use 12. The right choice depends on what is being optimised: specific work (engine size) or thermal efficiency (fuel burn). Real compressor and turbine losses change both answers.

blocks.markdown: The ideal Brayton cycle consists of isentropic compression, constant-pressure heat addition, isentropic expansion and constant-pressure heat rejection. In an air-standard analysis with constant specific heats, its thermal efficiency depends only on the pressure ratio $r_p$ and rises towards, but never reaches, 1 as $r_p$ increases (it is bounded by $1 - r_p^{-(k-1)/k}$). But the **specific work** does not: it has a maximum at an intermediate pressure ratio, because the turbine-entry temperature $T_3$ is limited by materials.

blocks.title: Thermal efficiency vs specific work
blocks.text: Thermal efficiency $\eta = w_{net}/q_{in}$ measures fuel use per unit of useful work. Specific work $w_{net}$ (kJ per kg of air) measures how much power a given airflow produces, and so how large and heavy the machine must be for a given power. They peak at different pressure ratios.

blocks.caption: Ideal cycle, $k = c_p/c_v = 1.4$ and $c_p = 1.005$ kJ/(kg K) for air. $T$ in K.

blocks.title: Optimum pressure ratio for maximum work
blocks.prompt: Air enters the compressor at $T_1 = 300$ K. Turbine-entry temperature is $T_3 = 1400$ K. For the ideal cycle, find the pressure ratio that maximises net work, the net work and the thermal efficiency. Assume $k = 1.4$, $c_p = 1.005$ kJ/(kg K).

steps.text: Isentropic temperatures at this pressure ratio, using $T_2 = T_1 r_p^{0.2857}$ and $T_4 = T_3 / r_p^{0.2857}$.

blocks.answer: r_p,opt = 14.82; w_net = 405.9 kJ/kg; thermal efficiency = 53.7%. Note that efficiency here is far below the Carnot value for 300 K and 1400 K.

blocks.title: Real cycle with component efficiencies
blocks.prompt: A gas turbine has $T_1 = 300$ K, $T_3 = 1400$ K and $r_p = 10$, compressor isentropic efficiency $\eta_C = 0.80$ and turbine isentropic efficiency $\eta_T = 0.85$. Find $T_2$, $T_4$, net work and thermal efficiency. Assume $k = 1.4$, $c_p = 1.005$ kJ/(kg K).

steps.text: Isentropic compressor exit temperature and then the actual one.
Isentropic turbine exit temperature and then the actual one.

blocks.answer: T2 = 649.0 K, T4 = 826.4 K, w_net = 225.8 kJ/kg, efficiency = 29.9% (compared with 48.2% ideal at the same pressure ratio).

blocks.caption: Effect of real-machine losses and turbine inlet temperature.

blocks.markdown: Because the net work is the difference of two large quantities (turbine work minus compressor work), a modest loss in each can wipe out a large fraction of the useful output. This is why gas turbines need efficient aerodynamic components: for $r_p = 10$, $T_3 = 1400$ K and efficiencies of 0.80 and 0.85 the net work falls from about 398 to 226 kJ/kg.

blocks.title: Which optimum?
blocks.text: Maximum specific work gives the smallest engine for a given power (important in aircraft); maximum thermal efficiency, which occurs at a higher pressure ratio, minimises fuel cost (important in baseload generation). Real engines choose between these, with the pressure ratio set by cost and weight.

items: $T_3$ is limited by blade materials and cooling, typically 1300 to 1600 K for modern industrial turbines.
The air-standard assumption (constant $c_p$) overstates efficiency; real values are lower because of variable $c_p$, pressure losses and heat addition from combustion.
Maximum specific net work occurs when the compressor temperature ratio $T_2/T_1$ equals $\sqrt{T_3/T_1}$ (that is, $T_2 = \sqrt{T_1 T_3}$), so $r_{p,opt}^{(k-1)/k} = \sqrt{T_3/T_1}$.
A gas turbine back-work ratio is about 40 to 60%, much higher than a steam plant.

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.text: Do not apply the efficiency to the temperature rise in the wrong direction: $T_2 = T_1 + (T_{2s}-T_1)/\eta_C$ (divide for the compressor), $T_4 = T_3 - \eta_T(T_3 - T_{4s})$ (multiply for the turbine). Use kelvin in all temperature ratios.

points: Ideal efficiency $1 - r_p^{-(k-1)/k}$ rises with $r_p$ but specific work peaks at $r_{p,opt} = (\eta_C\eta_T T_3/T_1)^{k/[2(k-1)]}$.
Real compressor and turbine efficiencies cut net work and thermal efficiency strongly.
Thermal efficiency measures fuel use; specific work measures engine size.
The pressure ratios for maximum work and for maximum efficiency are different.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes thermal efficiency from specific work for a gas turbine?

options.text: Efficiency is net work per unit air mass; specific work is net work per unit heat input
They are the same quantity expressed in different units
Efficiency is net work per unit heat input; specific work is net work per unit mass of air and sets the engine size for a given power
Specific work depends only on the compressor and efficiency only on the turbine

questions.correctOptionText: Efficiency is net work per unit heat input; specific work is net work per unit mass of air and sets the engine size for a given power

distractorRationale.b: They are different measures that peak at different pressure ratios.

questions.explanation: Thermal efficiency is the ratio $w_{net}/q_{in}$, which governs fuel consumption. Specific work $w_{net}$ per kg of air determines how much air flow, and so how large an engine, is required for a target power.

questions.stem: For an ideal Brayton cycle with constant specific heats, the pressure ratio that maximises net work is

distractorRationale.b: Missing the factor 2; this is the pressure ratio at which net work is zero.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong exponent; ignores the isentropic relation.
distractorRationale.d: Inverted ratio gives a value below 1.

questions.explanation: Setting $dw_{net}/dr_p = 0$ gives the compressor exit temperature equal to $\sqrt{T_1 T_3}$, so $r_p = (T_3/T_1)^{k/[2(k-1)]}$. The pressure ratio at which net work vanishes is $(T_3/T_1)^{k/(k-1)}$, the square of this.

questions.stem: A gas turbine's compressor isentropic efficiency falls from 0.88 to 0.78 at constant pressure ratio, inlet temperature and turbine-entry temperature. What happens to the compressor exit temperature and the net work?

options.text: The compressor exit temperature falls and the net work rises
The compressor exit temperature is unchanged and the net work falls
The compressor exit temperature rises and the net work rises
The compressor exit temperature rises and the net work falls

questions.correctOptionText: The compressor exit temperature rises and the net work falls

distractorRationale.a: This reverses the effect of irreversibility.
distractorRationale.c: The compressor absorbs more work, so net work falls.

questions.explanation: With lower $\eta_C$, $T_2 = T_1 + (T_{2s} - T_1)/\eta_C$ is higher and the compressor absorbs more work per kg. The turbine work is nearly unchanged, so the net work drops.

questions.stem: Engine A has a pressure ratio of 8 and a specific work of 330 kJ/kg; Engine B has a pressure ratio of 25 and a specific work of 280 kJ/kg with a higher thermal efficiency. A military aircraft needs a compact engine for a given thrust; a utility generates baseload power. Which choice is most appropriate?

options.text: Engine B for both because efficiency always dominates
Engine A for the aircraft (higher specific work gives a smaller engine) and Engine B for the baseload plant (lower fuel use)
Engine A for both because it has the higher work
Engine B for the aircraft and Engine A for the baseload plant

questions.correctOptionText: Engine A for the aircraft (higher specific work gives a smaller engine) and Engine B for the baseload plant (lower fuel use)

distractorRationale.a: Aircraft weight and size depend on specific work.
distractorRationale.c: Baseload plants value fuel cost, so efficiency matters more.

questions.explanation: Specific work sets the airflow, and so the size and weight, of an engine for a given power. Fuel cost depends on thermal efficiency, so the two applications weigh the two measures differently.

questions.stem: For a fixed compressor inlet temperature $T_1$, what happens to the pressure ratio for maximum specific work when the turbine-entry temperature $T_3$ is raised?

options.text: It decreases
It is unchanged
It increases
It becomes equal to 1

distractorRationale.a: The optimum depends on $(T_3/T_1)$ to a positive power.

questions.explanation: Since $r_{p,opt} = (T_3/T_1)^{k/[2(k-1)]}$ with a positive exponent, a higher $T_3$ raises the optimum pressure ratio. That is why advanced engines with hotter turbines use higher pressure ratios.

questions.stem: An ideal gas turbine has compressor inlet $T_1 = 288$ K and turbine entry $T_3 = 1200$ K. Taking $k = 1.4$, find the pressure ratio for maximum net work (dimensionless).
questions.explanation: $r_{p,opt} = (1200/288)^{1.75} = (4.1667)^{1.75} = 12.15$. The result is quoted in dimensionless and is of a physically reasonable magnitude.

questions.stem: Air at 290 K enters a compressor with pressure ratio 8 and isentropic efficiency 0.82. Using $k = 1.4$, find the actual compressor exit temperature in K.

A gas turbine operates with $T_1 = 295$ K, $T_3 = 1300$ K, pressure ratio 12, compressor efficiency 0.82 and turbine efficiency 0.88. Using $k = 1.4$ and $c_p = 1.005$ kJ/(kg K) (constant), calculate the thermal efficiency as a percentage.

A student claims that the best gas turbine is the one with the highest pressure ratio because the ideal cycle efficiency $1 - r_p^{-(k-1)/k}$ increases with $r_p$. Explain why this is incomplete, and describe what limits the useful pressure ratio.
markingGuide: Ideal efficiency indeed increases monotonically with $r_p$
Specific work has a maximum at an intermediate $r_p$, then falls to zero when compressor exit temperature reaches $T_3$
Net work per kg determines engine size and power for a given airflow
Turbine entry temperature $T_3$ limits the temperature rise in the combustor, so very high $r_p$ leaves little heat addition
Real component efficiencies reduce both efficiency and work, so net work can drop sharply at high $r_p$
Concludes that the choice is a trade between size/work and fuel efficiency
questions.explanation: Ideal efficiency alone ignores the fall in net work and the metallurgical limit on $T_3$. At very high pressure ratios the compressor absorbs almost all the turbine work, so net output vanishes.

questions.stem: Derive the pressure ratio for maximum net work of an ideal Brayton cycle in terms of $T_1$, $T_3$ and $k$. Then show how isentropic efficiencies $\eta_C$ and $\eta_T$ modify this result, and compute the optimum ratio for $T_1 = 300$ K, $T_3 = 1500$ K, $\eta_C = 0.85$ and $\eta_T = 0.90$ with $k = 1.4$.
markingGuide: Writes $w_{net} = c_p[(T_3 - T_4) - (T_2 - T_1)]$ with $T_2 = T_1 x$ and $T_4 = T_3/x$ where $x = r_p^{(k-1)/k}$
With efficiencies, the stage work is $\eta_T T_3(1 - 1/x) - T_1(x - 1)/\eta_C$ and $x = \sqrt{\eta_C \eta_T T_3/T_1}$
Notes the optimum falls when efficiencies fall
questions.explanation: Setting the derivative to zero gives $x = \sqrt{T_3/T_1}$ for the ideal cycle, and including $\eta_C \eta_T$ gives $x = \sqrt{\eta_C \eta_T T_3/T_1}$. For the given data $r_{p,opt} = 10.46$.
